item.title: Meta delays enforcement of new business terms amid publisher AI-scraping concerns
item.description:
Meta delays enforcement of new business terms amid publisher AI-scraping concerns

Meta announced a delay to the rollout of its revised business terms after worldwide publisher pushback over possible AI‑training scrapes of news sites.

🔍 Overview

  • The original effective date was October 30.
  • Enforcement has been pushed to November 20.
  • Delay is intended to give Meta time to explain what is changing and what is not.
  • Publishers warned the terms could let Meta scrape news sites for AI training.

📜 Business terms details

  • The draft terms appeared to give Meta permission to freely scrape news sites for AI training.
  • Meta later removed explicit language about “training” its products, but legal experts said the change may still allow scraping.

🗣️ Publisher and regulator response

  • The News/Media Alliance sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg demanding revisions, citing “severe harm” to publishers.
  • Digital advertisers and publishers in the European Union and the United Kingdom urged regulators to block the new terms.
  • Publisher backlash worldwide prompted Meta to delay the terms entirely.

🤝 Meta’s statement

  • spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge the November 20 start “allows more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not.”
  • Roberts added the delay will let Meta detail “how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences.”

💡 Why it matters

  • Scraping news content for AI models could affect revenue and control for publishers.
  • Robots.txt remains a tool for publishers to signal crawling preferences.
  • Regulatory attention in the EU and UK highlights growing scrutiny of large platforms’ data practices.

#Meta #AI #Publishing #Regulation

Source: Meta delays new business terms after publisher pushback on AI scraping

item.title: Meta Announces New Non‑Voting Share Class to Finance AI Initiatives
item.description:
Meta Announces New Non‑Voting Share Class to Finance AI Initiatives

Meta disclosed that it will issue a new class of non‑voting shares to fund its artificial‑intelligence strategy, potential acquisitions, and employee compensation.

🔍 Overview

  • Meta says it’s issuing a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives.
  • The new class will also fund acquisitions and employee compensation.
  • Trading of the non‑voting stock is slated to begin in 2027.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The announcement was made in Meta’s third‑quarter earnings report released on Wednesday.
  • The press release states: “The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant.”
  • CFO Susan Li said the shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.”
  • Meta expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion to $145 billion estimate.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The new share class provides Meta with an additional financing mechanism without diluting voting control.
  • It aligns capital allocation with the company’s aggressive AI roadmap, including recent launches such as the Muse AI agent.

🚀 Related AI Activity

  • Meta launched its AI agent, Muse, in September; the app quickly rose to the top of app stores and reached 10 million U.S. downloads.
  • Muse’s capabilities include cleaning email inboxes, booking restaurant reservations, and planning trips.

All statements are drawn directly from Meta’s press release and earnings call.

#Meta #AI #Finance #Shares

Source: Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push

item.title: Alex Gibney’s New Musk Documentary Sparks Platform Pushback
item.description:
Alex Gibney’s New Musk Documentary Sparks Platform Pushback

The latest Alex Gibney documentary about Elon Musk is now screening in select theaters. The film chronicles Musk’s past at xAI and SpaceX and asks why the public allowed him to amass so much power.

🎬 Film Details

  • The documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI/SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into his accumulation of power across governments worldwide.
  • Production began after Musk had already become a prominent figure in multiple technology sectors.

⚖️ Controversies & Platform Actions

  • Musk’s response has been stark: X blocked the feature from being advertised on the platform, and Musk, a self‑proclaimed “free speech absolutist,” threatened legal action against Gibney for producing a “hit piece.”
  • Advertisements for the film were initially missing from YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok.
  • Meta subsidiaries and YouTube later reversed their decisions, but TikTok has kept the ads blocked.
  • TikTok’s stance is notable given its indirect connections to the Trump administration via Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison.
  • David Ellison’s father, Oracle co‑founder Larry Ellison, a longtime Donald Trump supporter, led the consortium of investors that purchased TikTok’s US business late last year.
  • Ellison has reportedly promised Gibney that Musk will air on HBO (now part of Skydance) sometime next January.

📅 Release & Reception

  • The documentary is currently screening in select theaters.
  • It has faced an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The film highlights concerns about how much influence a single tech leader can wield over governments and the public narrative.
  • Musk’s aggressive pushback illustrates the tension between high‑profile documentaries and the subjects they profile, especially when those subjects control major platforms.

#ElonMusk #Documentary #TechPolitics #AILeadership

Source: The tech backlash is now in theaters

item.title: USA Today Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Use of News Articles
item.description:
USA Today Sues OpenAI Over Alleged Unauthorized Use of News Articles

USA Today Co has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that the company used the publisher’s copyrighted articles without permission.

🏛️ Overview

  • The complaint states that OpenAI copied hundreds of thousands of articles and other materials belonging to USA Today Co for AI training.
  • The lawsuit seeks damages exceeding $250 million and an injunction to stop the alleged infringement.

📄 Claims and Demands

  • USA Today claims the material was used without permission.
  • The company is demanding over $250 million in damages and seeks a court order to prevent further use.
  • The complaint does not settle whether OpenAI is legally obligated to pay for any alleged use.

⚖️ Legal Issues

  • The central question is whether OpenAI’s use of the articles violates copyright or falls under fair use.
  • Fair use is a US copyright doctrine that permits use of copyrighted material without prior permission under certain conditions.
  • AI firms argue that training models is a fair‑use activity because the system learns patterns and generates new output.
  • Publishers dispute this, asserting that large‑scale copying should not be deemed legal.
  • Courts consider four factors:
    1. Purpose of the use
    2. Character of the copyrighted work
    3. Amount and substantiality of the portion used
    4. Effect on the market value of the original work
  • Additional considerations may include whether the use is sufficiently transformative, the commercial context, and the impact on the publisher’s ability to profit from its reporting.

📈 Potential Impact

  • The decision could shape how AI companies collect and use news articles in the future.
  • The case adds to a broader legal debate about applying existing copyright rules to generative AI.
  • Similar lawsuits have been filed by other news organizations, including The New York Times, against OpenAI and Microsoft.

📰 Industry Concerns

  • Publishers rely on revenue from advertisements, subscriptions, and licensing.
  • There is concern that AI products could use content without paying, potentially reducing publishers’ income.
  • AI‑generated answers might keep users from visiting the original news site, further impacting revenue.
  • Licensing agreements are presented as one way for AI developers to obtain commercial access to news content.

#OpenAI #CopyrightLaw #NewsIndustry #AIlitigation

Source: USA Today sues OpenAI: USA Today vs OpenAI: Key questions over ChatGPT training data, news copyright and whether publishers should be paid for their work - The Economic Times
